#493. Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman

New archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. The ruler, known as Verica, played a pivotal role in events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. The findings challenge longstanding assumptions about early British history and the political influence of women during this period.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome, where the exiled ruler sought assistance from Emperor Claudius.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Ancient Evidence Challenges an Iron Age King's Identity

Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male.

"Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female."

Russell points to several pieces of evidence supporting this interpretation. One is the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter "a," a feature common among female names of the time. Other prominent examples include Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes (in Yorkshire), and Boudica, leader of the Iceni (in Norfolk).

All three rulers lived during roughly the same period. Boudica is the best known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60. However, Russell argues that Verica may have held even greater political power and influence.

Another important clue comes from coins issued under Verica's rule. These coins bear the Latin title "rex," traditionally translated as "king," which has contributed to the assumption that Verica was male. Russell explains that the title was not necessarily restricted to men.

"People also assume she was a 'he' because of the term 'rex' on coins, but rex is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous."

He continued: "The use of the Latin title rex on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor."

The artwork on Verica's coins provides another intriguing clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors commonly featured on coins produced by other British Iron Age rulers, Verica's coins show a figure with distinctly feminine characteristics.

"Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback."

The Forgotten Ruler Behind Rome's Invasion of Britain

Russell believes Verica's importance extended far beyond the ruler's identity. He argues that Verica may have been instrumental in helping Claudius successfully invade Britain.

Ancient Roman writers frequently portrayed Claudius as an ineffective emperor who was easily influenced by women and formerly enslaved people who had gained their freedom. This reputation may have shaped how historians described Verica's role in persuading him to invade.

Russell suggests that Cassius Dio's account reinforced this negative portrayal by presenting the invasion as a decision made under the influence of a woman. In reality, he argues, Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance.

"The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked. In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica's role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her on board ensured the project was a success, as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.

"The invasion was Claudius' great triumph -- it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it."

For Claudius, the conquest of Britain offered an opportunity to establish his reputation as a successful military commander. Verica's removal from power gave him a political justification for intervening, while the exiled ruler's knowledge of Britain may have helped the Roman forces achieve their objectives.

Could Rome's Conquest of Britain Have Been Avoided?

Although Verica was an important political figure in late Iron Age Britain, the ruler's influence has received relatively little attention compared with that of other prominent leaders.

Russell believes the archaeological evidence supports recognizing Verica as one of Britain's earliest and most significant female rulers. He also raises the possibility that the Roman invasion might never have occurred without Verica's exile and subsequent appeal to Claudius.

"We should take the archaeological evidence at face value" says Russell "and remember Verica as a female-king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed, fleeing to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place."

New Insights Into Women in Iron Age Britain

The findings build on earlier Bournemouth University research exploring the position of women in ancient British society.

Last year, a study involving Russell and other BU researchers uncovered evidence of a matriarchal society in Iron Age Britain. The research indicated that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage, suggesting that women occupied a central position in the social structure.

Together, these discoveries are prompting researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain, both within their communities and in the political decisions that shaped the region's future.

Russell's research on Verica is presented in the new book Caratacus: Great king of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902). The findings are also discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

#488. Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is Nvidia’s Stock

Jensen Huang is back, baby, and Wall Street is thrilled.

The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the past month.

Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia’s board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”

And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back—with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.

Many questions remain unanswered. What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect?

The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies. Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles—the index’s biggest decline since March 2020.

On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded.

Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amid the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it, actually. The stock is up.”

According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!

#485. Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today. A new scientific analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere during three major stages, while the deep oceans took much longer to catch up. In some cases, the delay stretched across hundreds of millions of years, with the final transition involving a gap of roughly 600 million years.

Two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation. Their findings challenge the traditional understanding of Earth's oxygen history by examining chemical evidence that reflects conditions in the ancient atmosphere rather than relying primarily on measurements of ocean chemistry.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Different Oxygen Timeline

Scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments. However, the amount of oxygen in seawater is influenced by many factors besides the atmosphere, including nutrient availability, biological productivity, ocean circulation, and the shapes of ocean basins. This makes ocean chemistry an imperfect guide to conditions in the air.

The researchers instead focused on sulfate, a chemical compound that can preserve a distinctive signal from atmospheric oxygen. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere produce an unusual shortage of the oxygen isotope oxygen-17. When sulfide minerals undergo weathering, this chemical fingerprint is transferred into sulfate, which can eventually become preserved in sedimentary rocks. By examining these signatures, scientists can gain a more direct picture of how atmospheric oxygen changed over time.

According to this evidence, Earth's first major increase in oxygen occurred during the Great Oxidation Event, between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen rose from less than one-millionth of today's concentration to somewhere between 0.1% and 10% of modern levels.

The second major increase took place approximately 1.3 billion to 1.0 billion years ago, followed by a third between 440 million and 410 million years ago. Both occurred earlier than conventional timelines suggest.

Under this interpretation, the well-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, traditionally dated to 800 million to 500 million years ago and 420 million to 360 million years ago, mainly reflect delayed changes in ocean oxygen levels. The oceans responded roughly 200 million and 30 million years after the corresponding atmospheric increases.

Earth's Atmosphere and Oceans Did Not Always Change Together

Despite these major increases, oxygen remained relatively scarce throughout much of Earth's history. Models based on the isotope evidence suggest that atmospheric oxygen during the middle Proterozoic reached only about 0.1% to 1% of present-day levels.

Another clue comes from the fossil record of charcoal. Because charcoal formation requires atmospheric oxygen concentrations of approximately three-quarters of modern levels, its absence from older rocks suggests that oxygen remained too scarce to support widespread burning. Charcoal first appears in the geological record around 420 million years ago.

The researchers also highlight a surprising relationship between oxygen in the atmosphere and oxygen in the oceans. Over extremely long periods, the two generally increased together. However, on timescales of around a million years, they could move in opposite directions.

When additional oxygen entered the oceans, it could react with accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, consuming oxygen in the process. These reactions could reduce the amount of oxygen remaining in the atmosphere.

As a result, some chemical signals previously interpreted as evidence of rising oxygen may actually record periods when atmospheric oxygen was declining. This possibility could change how scientists interpret major fluctuations in Earth's ancient oxygen record.

Oxygen-Rich Oases Existed Billions of Years Ago

The spread of oxygen through Earth's oceans was also far from uniform. The researchers describe two major sources of oxygen in seawater: oxygen produced locally by photosynthetic microorganisms and oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere.

The first process created isolated pockets of oxygen-rich water as early as 3 billion years ago, possibly even earlier. These small oxygenated environments existed during the Archean, when the atmosphere and most of the oceans still contained very little free oxygen.

As atmospheric oxygen levels gradually increased, oxygen entering seawater from the air became more important. Eventually, this atmospheric supply overtook local biological production as the dominant mechanism driving widespread ocean oxygenation.

Even then, the transformation was remarkably slow. According to the proposed timeline, the deep ocean did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago, long after oxygen had begun accumulating in the atmosphere.

How Rising Oxygen Changed the Evolution of Life

These findings also offer a new perspective on the relationship between oxygen and the evolution of complex organisms.

When Earth's atmosphere contained virtually no oxygen, its absence placed a major restriction on oxygen-dependent life. During the Proterozoic, increasing oxygen availability gradually made new environments accessible, although concentrations continued to fluctuate as early animals evolved.

Rather than acting as a single trigger for complex life, oxygen initially provided opportunities for biological innovation. Only after the third major atmospheric increase did higher oxygen levels become a powerful force supporting greater biological complexity.

This later transformation helped create conditions favorable for larger animals, more active predators, and organisms capable of occupying deeper marine environments.

The researchers acknowledge that important uncertainties remain. The available isotope record does not capture every change in detail, and absolute atmospheric oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain difficult to establish. Additional increases or decreases may have occurred without leaving sufficiently clear chemical evidence to identify them.

Nevertheless, the analysis proposes a major revision to the sequence of events that transformed Earth into an oxygen-rich planet. Rather than the oceans becoming oxygenated first and the atmosphere following, the evidence suggests that atmospheric oxygen increased well before the deep oceans responded.

That prolonged delay may have played an important role in shaping the environments where complex life emerged and evolved.

#482. Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV

In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.

Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.

A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.

The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing."

The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.

According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.

It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.

Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.

In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.

Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.

Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.

Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once."

Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.

"These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth."

#481. The Feds Left Iowans in the Dark About Plans to Blow Up Tons of Lead

On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.

“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.

Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.

Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.

Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.

“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.

The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.

“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.

The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.

The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.

In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.

The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.

The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)

Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.

“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”

For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.

“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”

#480. Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

Astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so quickly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

The discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe

During the first billion years after the Big Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

As galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

Because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

One reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Big, Too Fast

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

The black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

Astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Big Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how quickly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," says Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

The pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe."

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1]

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair

The discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

Using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

To investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

Obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

Fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," says Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2]

A New Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies

Exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," says Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

#475. This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a big impression on scientists. Although it is only about the size of a quarter, the spider has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.

The species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes. Its unusually large genome seems particularly fitting given Colbert's famously pompous television persona on the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report."

Many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween. But this particular spider stands out for something that cannot be seen with the naked eye: the extraordinary amount of DNA packed into its tiny body.

"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," said corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology.

According to Bond, this is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider belonging to this family. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity.

A Secretive Spider That Hunts From Underground

Visitors to the coastal dunes of Northern California may unknowingly pass close to these spiders without ever spotting one. Most of their lives unfold beneath the sand, where they remain hidden in carefully constructed burrows.

Female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged entrance that blends into its surroundings, allowing the spider to stay concealed while monitoring activity outside.

When an unsuspecting insect or other prey animal approaches, vibrations alert the spider to its presence. At precisely the right moment, the spider bursts through its hidden door to capture its next meal.

Although these spiders are skilled ambush predators, their venom poses no danger to humans. Bond noted that among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

A Spider Genome Bigger Than the Human Genome

The spider's DNA contains more surprises than its sheer size. Researchers found that its genome includes 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human cells, which are organized into 23 pairs.

However, having a larger genome does not necessarily mean having more genes. In this spider, approximately 77% of the genome consists of repetitive DNA sequences that appear many times throughout its genetic material.

The research also highlights an unusual feature of spider chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional repetitive DNA sequences associated with telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. This difference could help explain why spider chromosomes appear to evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life," Bond said.

Why Is the Spider Named After Stephen Colbert?

The story behind the spider's unusual scientific name dates back to 2008, when Stephen Colbert discovered that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young.

Not wanting to be left out, Colbert turned the situation into a comedy segment. During "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report," he publicly demanded that Bond name a spider in his honor.

Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti became Colbert's namesake in the spider world.

Rising Seas Threaten California's Trapdoor Spiders

Beyond revealing the spider's genetic peculiarities, the research could play an important role in protecting the species.

The genome sequencing effort is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative designed to build a collection of genomic information that scientists can use to guide conservation decisions.

Trapdoor spiders generally do not venture far from their burrows, making it difficult for populations to move between habitats. Because their coastal dune environments are already separated into isolated areas, researchers hope genetic information will help them identify distinct populations that may need special protection.

"We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond said. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species."

Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) is found only in coastal dunes along a limited stretch of Central California, extending from the San Francisco Bay area to Monterey.

This restricted range makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels could eliminate portions of its coastal habitat, while invasive species pose another significant danger.

"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond said.

Spider Venom Could Hold Clues to New Medicines

The potential benefits of studying this spider's genome extend beyond conservation and evolutionary biology. Scientists also hope that understanding spider genetics will help them explore the vast range of chemical compounds found in spider venom.

Some substances identified in spider venoms have shown promise as potential painkillers, while others could be useful in developing new ways to control agricultural pests.

With so many spider species still poorly understood at the genetic level, researchers believe their venoms may contain valuable compounds that have yet to be discovered.

"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," Bond said.

The study's additional authors include Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe and Oanh Nguyen of UC Davis; Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann and Merly Escalona of UC Santa Cruz; Robert D. Cooper of Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University; and H. Bradley Shaffer and Erin Toffelmier of UCLA.

The research received support from the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California through the state of California's State Budget Act of 2019, as well as from the National Science Foundation.

#474. Nvidia reinstates Huang as CEO: Trump, Musk, Altman react while the internet has jokes

Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he stepped down, and less than a week after the company's board said it had no intention of bringing him back. Reactions to Huang's return have been a mix of praise, criticism, and jokes, with several other tech executives rallying around him.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Nov. 12, a day after the board accepted it with immediate effect. He stepped down amid reports that he'd had extramarital affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and a Nvidia employee, with allegations of a third affair with another worker subsequently surfacing. His relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) drew particular scrutiny, as she was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips. She previously led Megaspeed, a company U.S. authorities have been investigating over concerns it smuggled advanced Nvidia chips to China in circumvention of U.S. restrictions.

While Huang said that he would be "honored" to return as CEO if asked, the board stated said on Nov. 17 that it did not plan to bring him back. Yet after reported pressure from President Donald Trump, the chipmaker has put Huang back in the top job after all. In a press release announcing Huang's reinstatement, Nvidia stated that it had based the decision on "input from senior levels of the United States government."

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," said Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones, who last week said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen."

Trump has been characteristically celebratory about Nvidia's decision, making several posts on his social media platform Truth Social on the topic. This included an edited image based on a photo of Trump after a shooter attempted to assassinate him in 2024. Originally posted by X account @grandoldmemes, the picture has been edited to show Huang holding a red bra aloft as a Nvidia banner is displayed in the background.

Calling Huang's reinstatement an "absolutely GREAT decision" (emphasis original), Trump stated that having him installed as Nvidia's CEO is vital to the U.S. economy.

"The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," wrote Trump. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security…. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure."

The U.S. president also spoke about Huang's reinstatement in a phone call to CNBC on Monday.

"I think he's gonna start off at an almost higher level," Trump said. "He's apologised for [his] indiscretion, which was unfortunate. Probably that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas. Now [CNBC host Jim] Cramer would not know that because he’s a very, very, very committed person. But sex sells."

Trump's on-and-off ally Elon Musk also celebrated Huang's return, reposting Nvidia's announcement on X and writing that "the mistake has been corrected." Last week, Musk stated that he was signing a petition to reinstate Nvidia's then-ousted CEO.

"Everyone I know at Nvidia wanted Jensen back and it shows," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO continued, sharing a post from investor Gavin Baker. In it, Baker shared images of people crowding around Huang and applauding him on his return to Nvidia's offices.

"Grateful to the President, everyone in the administration, everyone who signed the petition, everyone who supported Jensen publicly, everyone who called the board, everyone on the board who fought for him, everyone," Baker wrote. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Musk himself was ousted as CEO of X.com in 2000 after it merged with Confinity, the company behind PayPal. He had reportedly wanted to phase out the PayPal name in favor of X.com, despite concerns about its explicit connotations.

Various other prominent figures in tech have also voiced support for Huang's return, several of whom have previously faced comparable turmoil at their own companies.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared to express approval for Huang's reinstatement, publishing a post on X that simply read, "Jensen!" Altman went through a similar incident when OpenAI's board fired him in 2023, accusing him of lying, retaliating against critics, and creating a "toxic atmosphere." Despite these allegations, Altman was ultimately reinstated after days of outcry from supporters.

Meanwhile, Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao posted to X that he was "glad to see @JensenHuang back," resharing his previous reaction that it was "a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign." Zhao resigned from his role as CEO of Binance and pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program in 2023, serving a four-month prison sentence. However, he remains Binance's majority shareholder and retains significant influence over the global cryptocurrency exchange.

Uber co-founder and former CEO Travis Kalanick weighed in as well, stating that he would "always sign up to serve" Huang. Kalanick had previously posted support for reinstating Huang at Nvidia and asked followers to share "some great ideas for how to 'persuade' the Nvidia board to bring Jensen back."

"Jensen is a great man, flawed like the rest of us, but at the same time the best amongst us," Kalanick posted to X on Monday. "The world and humanity needs him to fight for a shot at liberty, a counterweight to techno-authoritarianism."

Kalanick resigned from his role as Uber CEO in 2017 after demands from multiple major investors. This came after Kalanick took a leave of absence amid allegations of a misogynistic workplace culture. Though one of the investors sued Kalanick for fraud later that year, the ousted CEO remained on Uber's board until resigning in 2019.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov also celebrated Huang's return, posting "Jensen's back" with a party popper emoji. He then joked about the situation, writing that "Nvidia's board finally accepted that a CEO has to evaluate Chinese models personally. You can't delegate that."

Durov was ousted from his former role as CEO of Russian social media platform VK in 2014 after the board said it had accepted a resignation he'd submitted and failed to withdraw. Durov claimed the resignation had been an April Fools' joke and suggested that his firing was politically motivated.

Given their own personal experiences, it's no surprise that many former and current tech executives have supported Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO. Other reactions have been a mixed bag — some celebrating the news, some condemning it, and others simply enjoying the jokes and memes.

"Reinstating Huang is a disaster for corporate governance and even the rule of law, but it is objectively very very funny," author and tech reporter David Z. Morris posted to X.

Some have also noted the timing of Huang's temporary ousting, joking that he deliberately orchestrated several days away from work in order to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

It's been a tumultuous few weeks for Nvidia, and it's unclear how the company plans to move forward at this stage. However, whatever happens, the jokes will likely continue for a while.

#472. How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump

Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior, Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped 6 percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, the odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to coming back, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when Trump threw his support behind the former CEO.

But Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode also identified clusters of trades that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and long-shot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and a professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says he figured that people like Trump, who had an interest in boosting Nvidia’s stock price, would successfully pressure the board to reinstate Huang. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “pee in your brain.”)

“It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

#471. Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

Carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

The discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

Beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

Scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

Recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

These plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

When that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam says.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature

Hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

The Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," says Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core."

Although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created."

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

"All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets."

Scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The new findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially important contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

According to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth

Despite the intriguing evidence, important questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

"We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

They also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

"It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting."

The study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.

#468. EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit

The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed on "landmark" deals on youth mobility and trade. Leaders on both sides praised the agreement as they seek to rebuild ties.

European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.

This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.

During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.

Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.

He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."

Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."

He went further and said "Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.

Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."

She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."

Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.

She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."

Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it."

In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.

"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.

The three key agreements establish ways to:

The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.

No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students

"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.

Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,."

On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.

They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.

According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.

Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.

The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.

#467. Inside Nvidia, Not Everyone Is Celebrating Jensen Huang’s Return

Jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters.

But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues.

Some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct. Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged.

“Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.”

Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

When Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.)

US president Donald Trump said he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and says they expect him to exercise better judgment going forward.

Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on plans to step up corporate governance.

It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The company’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at Nvidia,” the chipmaker’s official website declares.

A public petition campaign known as Stand With Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce.

But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment.

Huang’s supporters have praised how he made the company feel like a “big super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker.

There are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process.

But for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.”

Several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged. Two former employees say that he regularly raised his voice at workers, sometimes in ways they found belittling.

Other employees were more concerned about whether Nvidia’s board would hold Huang accountable for allegedly misleading the directors about his affairs. “That’s something we can’t have,” one employee says.

Another source of frustration for Nvidia workers has been the growing influence of Huang’s two children and son-in-law, who all hold senior titles at the chipmaker. In March, his daughter, Madison Huang, scolded a colleague on a call with about 100 other employees, according to a participant who didn’t believe the anger was warranted. “I’m disappointed you asked that. Are you fucking stupid?” the employee recalls Madison saying in response to a question about workshops on OpenClaw technology scheduled for an upcoming Nvidia conference. “Your mom can build a claw.”

Madison and her brother, Spencer Huang, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Praveen Mhapsekar, a senior system software engineer who separated with Nvidia last week after disputes with his managers and HR, says he and colleagues stopped feeling comfortable complaining about practices that concerned them because of the trouble they believe it brought on themselves.

“This organization requires greater discipline and structured processes,” he says. One of the world’s most valuable companies “cannot be managed like a private startup operating out of a garage, where personal influence takes precedence over established procedures.”

Huang’s return doesn’t eliminate the prospect of Nvidia evolving to quell frustrations. But with internal issues more public than ever before, maybe the days of one big family all cheering along together are mostly gone.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode and Hugo Lowell.
