#432. 'We slept here': Flight delays linger as airlines recover from ground stop, but schedule improves Monday

U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware.

Over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop.

On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve.

"We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that the Transportation Security Administration wouldn't let her through security at first.

"It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy said Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

President Donald Trump said Monday he didn't "take any responsibility" for the ground stop.

Shortly after the ground stop, Duffy said he was asking Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

"Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," said Reps. Rick Larsen, D.-Wash., ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Andre Carson, D.-Ind., ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, in a joint statement.

#428. Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond

Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.

Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

#427. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

This article was originally published in German.

#425. The best wireless earbuds weve ever tested (and continue to love)

If you're looking for a new pair of earbuds, we have good news: You have a lot of options. The bad news? You have a lot of options, and your decision can get overwhelming, fast. Wasn't life easier when iPhones came with a free pair of earbuds?

While you can still find wired earbuds that plug in and go, the market is flooded with high-quality wireless options. Now, you'll find models with advanced active noise cancellation, multi-point pairing, high-resolution audio support, and extra-long battery life. To help you choose, Mashable's audio experts put the best wireless earbuds from Apple, Bose, Sony, and other top brands to the test.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

The best wireless earbuds range anywhere from $10 to $1,000, especially if you're going for professional-grade studio earphones. And if you care about active noise cancellation, you can easily spend $300 — that's the price of peace and quiet. You can also get hyperspecialized models like sleep earbuds, bone-conduction earbuds for working out, and open earbuds for transparency. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

In 2026, our top picks for earbuds are the Sony WF-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd gen), and Panasonic Technics AZ100s, which provide outstanding sound quality and ANC. But keep in mind that these models will run you $299 to $329. While we stand by the value of everything on this list, we know that spending over $300 on a pair of earbuds is a lot to stomach. That's why we've also included more budget-friendly wireless earbuds under $100 that still deliver excellent performance.

Ready to start shopping now? Here are our favorite wireless and noise-cancelling earbuds as of November 2026.

Read our full review of the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds.

Anyone looking for the all-around best experience: Sony's new XM6 earbuds are the follow-up we've been waiting for from the brand. Though they cost a lot, they justify their price point in an excellent performance on all fronts, which brings some of the best ANC, sound quality, design, and ease of use to one elegant package.

Sony built a reputation for providing some of the best sound quality available in the game, and while we still think the Technics on this list eke out a better performance, Sony's overall package is unrivaled.

The earbuds sound great out of the box, but the 10-band equalizer gives the user plenty of options for customization. Whether we listened to classic rock or straight-up classical concertos, these earbuds made music sound immersive, rich, and clear. To supplement the great sound quality, Sony also stepped up its ANC game from the previous gen, resulting in the best ANC we've ever encountered on a pair of earbuds. Though we wish it were adjustable (especially at this price point), if you're looking to block out the world around you as much as possible, we think these perform even better than our former favorites, the Bose QC Ultra 2 buds.

Where Bose has Sony beat is in comfort. Sony did redesign the shape of its earbuds from the previous gen, helping provide an even more comfortable and flush fit. Still, Bose's stability band still takes the cake for the best fit we've ever experienced — but Sony is closing that comfort gap.

Read our full review of the Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds.

Audiophiles first and foremost: If you want to hear every note in perfect crisp detailed sound, the Panasonic's Technics EAH-AZ100 make music better thanks to their magnetic fluid drivers. Whether you want a fully customizable experience by adjusting your bass and treble, or you just want to pop in your buds and experience delicious spatial audio without the fuss, the Technics offer users both.

Panasonic blew us away with its Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds. If you've ever thought that earbuds can't deliver the same potent sound quality as over-ear headphones, then let the AZ100s prove you wrong. The buds come with four different ear tips that range from extra small to large, delivering a snug and secure fit suitable for even those with small or narrow ears who struggle to find earbuds that fit. That being said, they aren't the most comfortable headphones we've ever tested (nothing beats the Bose QuietComfort Ultras), as they get uncomfortable after a couple of hours of wear.

However, what you're really after here is the incredible sound quality of the Technics. Music just sounds better on the AZ100 earbuds. The earbuds deliver music as close to the source as possible. While listening to James Brown's "The Boss," the song sounded rich and textured, with layers of horn and deep bass bursting through. Plus, it picks up on the most subtle details, like in "Angel Of My Dreams" by Jade, the soft shuttering of cameras flashing on the backing track rang through in crisp detail.

Plus, these headphones have impressive active noise cancellation. While testing them on a trip to New York, they blocked out the clatter of the subway and ruckus of noisy streets. With such excellent ANC, nothing distracts from the superior audio quality. The three-way multipoint connection is another huge advantage of these headphones. I could seamlessly switch between my iPhone, iPad, and MacBook Pro without having to open the app.

Not to mention, these earbuds have killer battery life. They last for 10 hours with an additional 28 hours available with the charging case.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds (2nd gen).

Long-haul travelers, students, or anyone who can't get earbuds to fit quite right: For those who value noise cancellation and all-day wear above all else, the $299 Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds (2nd gen) are worth the investment. With spatial audio and some of the best ANC we've encountered, these earbuds deliver immersive sound that envelopes you in your music.

Over-ear headphones are the typical pick for those who want the best noise cancellation, but these days, you're no longer limited if you prefer earbuds but still want top-tier ANC.

Bose's second iteration of its QuietComfort Ultra earbuds doesn't change too much from the original, with the main improvements coming in the form of wireless charging, improved speech clarity on calls, and better adaptive ANC, but we also noticed some minor improvements to the sound profile, which also did a great job of sounding full and resonant right out of the box.

Where these earbuds really shine, however, is in their name: it's their fit and noise cancellation. Though they only have three sizes of ear tips and stability bands, the design of these earbuds allows for a fit that's both secure and comfortable enough to wear for hours on end, which isn't a given with earbuds. The noise cancellation impresses, too, even without any music playing, thanks to the eight microphones packed into these buds. Common household sounds like air conditioning, neighbors, and other people existing in your space all but disappear with the ANC bumped all the way up. If you don't like that much blockage, you can turn on transparency mode or manually adjust the level of ANC.

So what are the downsides? Besides being priced like a premium pair of earbuds (which, to be fair, they are in their performance), the six-hour battery life is starting to lag behind competitors. Plus, the equalizer is less sophisticated than what you'll find on other earbuds, and the touch controls weren't quite as seamless as we want on $300 earbuds. Still, for the combo of noise-cancelling and comfort, we can't choose a better pair of earbuds.

Read our full review of the Apple AirPods Pro 3.

Apple fans: Apple device owners will appreciate how easily these earbuds pair with multiple devices, as well as their impressive active noise cancellation and the many ways they can be used.

The AirPods Pro pop up on most best of lists, and though we've always been fans, the third generation takes these earbuds to a new level.

At the most basic level, these earbuds perform well in all the ways you'd want them to: the sound profile is robust and clear, the noise cancellation truly silences the world around you, and they pair easily to Apple devices. With this generation, Apple bumped up these buds' battery life to eight hours per charge, putting them firmly on the higher end of what's available on the market.

Then, there are the extra features. Apple included a built-in heart rate monitor, which can be used when you track your workouts with the Fitness app. How did it perform? "Perfectly," according to Mashable contributor Adam Doud's review. "I checked the heart rate against another device...and in every instance, the heart rate from the AirPods Pro 3 was within a beat or two per minute of the other device, so that speaks very well for its accuracy." Along with the IP57 water- and sweat-resistance and five sizes of ear tips for finding just the right fit, the AirPods Pro have become a much better pair of earbuds for working out this generation.

Finally, the live translation. At the time of writing, it's available in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and English from the UK. Doud wrote that it worked fairly accurately (as compared to movie subtitles) with a one to two second delay, making the feature viable for real-time use.

At $249, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are on par (and even cheaper) than other premium competitors. So what's the catch? Well, for anyone looking to fine-tune their own audio experience, there's no companion app or custom equalizer, but for everything else you get, the trade-off may well be worth it.

Read our full review of the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case.

Apple fans on a budget: The AirPods Pro 3 are great, but with the addition of better noise cancellation, a wireless charging case, volume controls on the stem, and live translation to the AirPods 5 model, you can get a very similar experience for $100 cheaper, making this the best value option for Apple-centric users.

These are also a great pick for anyone who wants earbuds that sit in between an in-ear and open earbud, as they don't have an ear tip that's situated in the ear canal, but rather rest near it as a traditional earbud would.

Apple pulled a rare move by lowering the prices on the AirPods 5 while adding more features, which made our job pretty easy in recommending them. They come with 50 percent better ANC than the AirPods 4, while being $149 compared to the 4's $179. Despite being a semi-in-ear model, they provide a surprising amount of sound control. Mashable Senior Editor Stan Schroeder wrote in his review that though they struggled on higher-pitched sounds, "on an actual plane, I realized they did a pretty good job of reducing both the engines' drone and the passengers' chatter."

He was also particularly impressed by how they sounded for live performances, as open earbuds tend to let the wider soundstage shine more than traditional in-ear buds, which might emphasize clarity and bass — he appreciated the width of the sound. These earbuds also come with the Live Translation feature found on the AirPods Pro 3, which allows for language translation in real time, as well as a volume sliding control on the stem. You'll miss out on the more expensive earbuds' built-in heart rate monitor and Hearing Protection feature, but if neither is too important to you, you'd likely be better off saving the cash. The biggest difference besides the wear is perhaps the battery life: where the AirPods Pro 3 get eight hours per charge, you'll have to settle for five hours per charge with the AirPods 5, but you will have a smaller carrying case than the Pros.

Bargain hunters: Finding a solid pair of budget earbuds is all about balance, and the EarFun Air Pro 4 exemplify that perfectly. While not the absolute cheapest pair of earbuds you could buy, they're still less than $100 and perform at the level of earbuds double their price. For anyone looking for the best value noise-cancelling earbuds, these are our top pick.

The EarFun earbuds don't fall into the pitfalls of other budget buds on the market. Yeah, you'll pay more than $50 pair (but only slightly if you grab them during one of their frequent sales). What you'll get in return is affordable earbuds that can adeptly handle a multipoint connection, feature a well-rounded sound profile with variation thanks to the in-app equalizer, and a battery life that can likely power you through most, if not all, of your workday.

The efficacy of the active noise cancellation is an especially standout feature of these earbuds, thanks to the absence noise breakthrough or strong hissing to supplement the power of the ANC. (Usually, one or both can be found on cheaper earbuds.) EarFun could've stopped there, but these earbuds also offer manually adjustable ANC, which isn't even a given on premium noise-cancelling earbuds. While not every level of adjustment is worth writing home about, it's still a nice addition.

Five sizes of ear tips ranging from XS to XL help with a comfortable fit and providing the best passive noise cancellation possible. Overall, these earbuds start to verge on too good to be true for their price point. The one major flaw we could find is that their on-ear touch controls verged on being both under-and overly sensitive, causing our tester to prefer toggling them off entirely in the companion app. Still, if there was one feature EarFun was going to flop on, this is maybe the least annoying of the bunch.

Read our full review of the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds.

Restless sleepers in noisy nighttime environments: Within a few months, Soundcore turned around and upgraded its already excellent Sleep A30 earbuds, bringing the Sleep A30 Special earbuds to the scene. For anyone who needs noise cancellation to help them get to sleep, the Sleep A30 Specials are basically your only option — thankfully, they're also one of the best valued options.

The major names in the sleep earbuds space are Ozlo and Soundcore. While Ozlo is known for being made by former Bose engineers, the $349 earbuds come at a huge price point — especially considering their lack of features in comparison to Soundcore's offerings.

Most notably, the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds offer active noise cancellation, the only sleep earbuds to do that other than their predecessor, the Sleep A30 earbuds. Even better, they do it at a significantly lower price point than the Ozlo buds at $229.99. While it's still a decent price to pay for earbuds solely designed for sleep, relatively speaking, A30 Specials offer some of the best value by far due to the feature set.

In addition to the ANC, the companion app offers several white noise options, including customizable soundscapes and Calm app meditations. If you prefer to stream your own audio, Soundcore's Bluetooth streaming with ANC on can last through an entire night of sleep (an upgrade from the regular A30 earbuds). The brand also recently added an update to the app that allows users to toggle on a timed turn-off for their audio, instead of the sleep detection option that existed at the earbuds' release.

These earbuds' case also monitors the environment in real time to provide adaptive snore masking, should the user toggle that option on. Standard features that exist on other earbuds will also be found on these buds, including a built-in alarm, sleep tracking data, and touch controls.

Read our full review of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds.

Runners, gym rats, and fitness fans: If you don't want to be bothered by loose or ill-fitting headphones while lifting or on a run, go for a pair that won't budge. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 fit snuggly within the ear, but the extra ear hook adds an extra level of security. For iOS users, these connect instantly, but even Android users can benefit from a quick Bluetooth connection, too.

When you're on the go and want to stay hands-free, the Powerbeats Pro 2 have external controls for answering calls or playing music. Plus, the Powerbeats bring crisp sound that helps you block out sound when you'd rather focus on your workout and not the gym crowd around you. Not to mention, the Powerbeats also include a heart rate monitor for real-time readings.

The Powerbeats Pro have earned a permanent spot in my gym bag. They fit snuggly within the ear and with the ear hooks don't budge, no matter how sweaty I get or how I move through my workouts. As an iPhone user, they're a dream to connect, automatically doing so whenever I take them out of the case.

With their noise-cancelling capabilities, they're able to block out the noise of the gym or the outdoors. But if you want to be able to hear the world around you for safety, you can swap into Transparency Mode. The sound is clear and consistent. Is it the best sound quality I've tested? No, but it's still pretty great.

The on-ear earbud controls are great. The Beats Fit Pro suffered from overly sensitive controls, causing me to accidentally end a call or two. But the controls on the Powerbeats Pro 2 don't get set off by accidentally brushing them. The battery life on the Powerbeats Pro 2 is incredible, up to 45 hours with the case. I think I went a full month without charging them — even with daily use.

It actually wasn't love at first wear with the Powerbeats. At first, they're pretty awkward figuring out how to fit the bud in your ear and then hooking them around. Both my colleague, Bethany Allard, and I tested the Powerbeats and struggled with the learning curve of getting them to fit, and it was a bad first impression of the Beats. While I do like how customizable they are with five different ear tips, navigating their fit is difficult at first.

However, after a few months of use, I realized the Powerbeats Pro 2 became my go-to gym earbud. While other earbuds didn't sound as good, started to slip out when things got sweaty, or required frequent charging, I always returned to the Powerbeats Pro 2.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort earbuds.

Anyone who wants budget-friendly from a premium brand: If you want good-quality sound but don’t want to spend over $200, the Bose QuietComfort is an affordable answer to the brand’s lineup. They’re focused on a great fit, as they not only come with multiple ear tips but multiple bands that can be changed out on the earbuds for a better fit on the crest of your ear.

The accompanying app lets you adjust audio levels, but you won’t need to, as these earbuds make all your music sound better. They’re reliable, have a long battery life, and are sure to please the pickiest of audiophiles.

I’ve sung the praises of the QuietComfort Ultra, but Bose’s latest earbuds, the entry-level QuietComfort, are also fantastic, especially with their under-$200 price tag. Even after adjusting the ear tips and bands, I didn’t find the fit on these quite as secure as the Ultras. However, my colleague Bethany Allard, who also tested the QuietComfort earbuds, said they were the best earbuds that have ever fit her.

The QuietComfort’s sound quality is just phenomenal. With these earbuds, listening to Ethel Cain’s A House in Nebraska immersed me in the orchestrations. When Brick House by The Commodores came on, the earbuds elevated the snappy drum beats so that I may have been listening live.

The noise cancellation on the QuietComfort earbuds isn’t as sophisticated as the Ultras; I found they had more sound leakage and that classic ANC buzz when I was in noisy environments. However, the ANC on these is still great, especially in quiet spaces.

One tiny beef I have with the Bose QuietComfort earbuds is that they require a different app than the standard Bose one. This is annoying if you’re an existing Bose user and need to download another app; plus, this earbud app just isn’t as good as Bose’s flagship app.

All in all, these are a solid pair of headphones that, for $179, are an unbeatable value.

Read our full review of the Bose Ultra Open (2nd gen).

Anyone who finds earbuds too uncomfortable: If you want a pair of everyday earbuds with an open design, the latest Bose Ultra Open earbuds will be your best bet. Yes, $300 is a hefty investment, but they have the best sound quality of any open earbuds we've tried. Plus, Bose's clip-on design can't be beat, from the comfort to the colorways.

The open earbuds trend has taken off in the past few years for anyone who craves some more awareness when listening to their audio. Maybe it's because you don't want to totally feel siloed in your own world; maybe it's convenient for exercise, more comfortable, or simply safer with their heightened awareness. Whatever your reason for wearing them, in our testing, we found the second-generation Bose Ultra Open earbuds are the best choice for most folks.

We were already fans of the sound quality of the first-generation Bose open buds, but the second generation adds more bass and depth, making it the superior open earbud listening experience. Bose also nails the design. The clip is secure, easy to adjust, and comfortable enough to wear for hours. You'd think at least one of those areas would suffer, but Bose strikes the balance. Rounding out the top-tier design are the excellent color selection (black, white smoke, limited-edition cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink) and the best tactile controls you'll find on any pair of earbuds, thanks to the button on the top of the clip mechanism's back side. These buds also come with an IPX4 water and sweat resistance rating, so you're cleared for workouts.

So what's the catch? Well, they're expensive as hell, even for regular noise-cancelling earbuds. If these lean too pricey, our former top pick, the Shokz OpenDots One, is still a worthwhile (and more affordable) choice for clip-on earbuds.

Read our full review of the Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro.

Versatility is key: The Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro are the jack of all (earbud) trades, master of none. They're the only real option if you want to keep open and noise cancelling earbuds with you on the go without carrying around, or paying or, two completely separate pairs of earbuds. They're not the best in either department, but they're pretty solid in both, making them an excellent option for those who value convenience above all else.

Admittedly, the pool of options is pretty much limited to the AeroFit 2 Pro when considering dual-form earbuds — unless you count the noise-reduction features on Shokz OpenFit Pro. For true noise cancellation and open form wear however, you'll have to look to the Soundcore buds.

That criteria on its own doesn't earn these earbuds a spot on our list, though. Soundcore followed through on their innovative design by producing earbuds that actually perform well, too, even with their flaws. Let's start with the weakest point: these earbuds don't come with interchangeable ear tips (á la the AirPods 4), instead staying in place with an adjustable ear hook that looks them into the noise cancelling or open mode. While still relatively comfortable, it does mean that they suffer somewhat on the passive noise cancellation front. Paired with just-okay ANC, you won't be getting the best noise blocking out there — expect to be able to somewhat make out conversations of coworkers or fellow cafe-goers, though both will be dampened.

Still, if the best ANC isn't a top priority, this a fairly easy feature to overlook. Especially when a quick adjustment of the ear hook, you suddenly have the best transparency mode possible — an open-ear design. Soundcore has plenty of experience making solid open earbuds, so it came as no surprise that the sound on these was clear, relatively robust, and noticeably varied, especially with equalizer adjustments. The ear hook kept them sturdy and in place, making these IP55 dust and water-resistance rated buds an excellent option for wear while working out or simply staying aware while out and about.

There are two overarching types of earbuds: wireless and wired. While those descriptors are self-explanatory, let's get into the specifics of both.

Wireless earbuds connect to devices via Bluetooth for cordless usage. These earbuds range from $20 budget models to high-end models with active noise cancellation. While they don't require a wire to connect to a device, some wireless earbuds still have a wire that might go around the back of the neck to connect the buds.

While earbuds traditionally don't provide the passive noise cancellation of over-the-ear headphones, wireless models often feature ANC, which electronically blocks out background noise. With wireless headphones, you need to consider the battery life. Most models should have an eight-hour or more battery life before they need to be recharged.

Wired earbuds are the original model: two buds connected by a wire to your audio source. While they once felt high-tech, they're pretty basic now. Wired earbuds with active noise cancellation are basically non-existent, other than Bose's newest release.

The biggest positive of wired headphones is that they don't need to be charged. They're a great backup option to keep in your bag in case your usual wireless headphones or earbuds run out of charge.

We added the new Apple AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case to this guide in October following their September 2026 release as a cheaper alternative for Apple users, or for folks who don't prefer the ear tip fit of the AirPods Pro 3.

After extensive testing, Mashable Lead Shopping Reporter Bethany Allard rounded up the best sleep earbuds. You can read her full guide, but as of February 2026, we've added the Anker Soundcore Sleep A30 Special to this guide, which Allard says are the best sleep earbuds for most people. Also in February 2026, we added the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds as our top pick for the best overall earbud, and removed the previous generation, the WF-1000XM5, as the best Sony earbud.

Bose recently announced two new open earbuds: the Ultra Open (2nd gen) and Sport Open. We'll be testing them out to see how they compare to the Shokz earbuds in this guide. Bose also released a new pair of wired noise-cancelling earbuds, which are a breakthrough in the wired earbuds market.

With the announcement that Bose is acquiring Skullcandy and the release of the Noise Master Buds Open earbuds with Sound by Bose, we'll be testing more Bose-powered audio products not directly from the brand.

If you're just looking for a pair of everyday wireless earbuds, all but one of the models in this guide will check that box. (We formerly included the Marshall Mode earbuds for folks who preferred a wired option, but have since removed them from our guide as the version we tested is difficult to find in stock these days.)

If you're looking for the highest quality wireless earbuds, you can't go wrong with the Sony WF-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Ultra, Apple AirPods Pro 3, and Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds, our most recent recommendations in 2026. All of these wireless earbuds feature elite noise cancellation, stellar sound, long battery life, and a comfortable fit for extended wear.

Though most earbuds are now wireless, this ultimately comes down to preference. If you have a tighter budget or don't want to worry about the battery running low all the time, wired earbuds are a great option. With that said, it is significantly harder to find wired earbuds with active noise cancellation. At the time of writing, the only pair with both wired connectivity and ANC both is from Bose — we're still in the process of testing them out.

To help you decide, we put a range of wireless earbuds to the test to determine which are worth your money. Whether you're simply looking for earbuds to get you through the work day, a pair to take with you on a flight, or a pair that you can live in 24/7, we have a set of buds for you. And if nothing on this list stands out to you, you can always expand your search to headphones as well.

As long as they're Bluetooth-compatible, these earbuds should connect to any smartphone, tablet, or laptop regardless of operating system. All of the earbuds on this list work equally well across iOS and Android systems with one exception — Apple AirPods.

Our favorite AirPods, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are great and will connect to an Android device, but you won't get the same ease of connectivity or full array of features. However, other earbuds like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds and the Panasonic Technics AZ100 feature Android apps so you can experience their full range of features on an Android device.

Each pair of earbuds selected for this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. Along with wireless earbuds tested specifically for this article, we also combed through our existing reviews to pick the best of the best earbuds for 2026. In addition to the bang for your buck, when testing earbuds, we consider criteria such as:

For each of our earbuds, we do our best to run their battery life out and test it against the stated battery life. All ANC earbuds are used with ANC, and while each tester defers to their preferred volume, we do try to average around the 50% mark when in use.

We tested out these earbuds with a variety of songs, from live performances to bass-heavy electronic music, R&B, rock, and folksy guitar songs. We evaluated how they sounded out of the box, along with any EQ presets or custom controls. Realistically, you'll make calls when using your earbuds, which is why we put each of these earbuds through a call test, making sure the person on the other end of the phone could hear us clearly and consistently.

Though this category can be subjective, we made sure each of our selections at least had several different ear tip sizes and were comfortable to wear for stretches of three hours or more. We also evaluate features like cleverly placed touch controls and stabilizers for keeping earbuds in place, both during casual use and exercise.

Any feature that made the earbuds stand out and also performed consistently well earned points in this category. For example, in addition to a rich out-of-the box sound profile, the Sony earbuds had an incredibly customizable and user-friendly experience with the in-app equalizer.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for five years at Mashable.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

#420. Grubhub is giving away a full year of Grubhub+ for free this Black Friday — how to claim

TL;DR: Through Dec. 7, first-time Grubhub customers (plus invited existing users) can get one year of Grubhub+ for free — with no promo code required.

Delivery fees can easily turn a $15 takeout order into a $28 regret, so getting a whole year of free delivery on the house is tough to beat. Through Dec. 7, this Grubhub+ Black Friday deal gives eligible diners a full 12 months of Grubhub+ for free — with no promo code required.

Normally, Grubhub+ runs $9.99 per month (which adds up to nearly $120 over a year) or $90 if you pay annually. That saves you up to $120 in membership fees alone.

Once your free year is active, your account unlocks the full lineup of Grubhub+ perks across both Grubhub and Seamless:

$0 delivery fees on eligible standard orders from participating Grubhub+ restaurants and stores (including standard delivery on eligible Instacart-powered grocery orders), as long as your order meets the merchant's minimum subtotal before tax, tip, and fees.

Lower service fees and discounted priority delivery (at the reduced rate shown at checkout) on eligible restaurant orders that meet the subtotal minimum.

5% back in Grubhub+ Credit on eligible restaurant pickup orders, calculated on your food subtotal before tax, tip, and fees.

Exclusive member-only offers on qualifying restaurant orders (and your perks also carry over to Seamless).

Before you sign up, there are a few eligibility rules and fine-print details worth keeping in mind so you don't get hit with an unexpected charge down the road:

The offer is strictly for first-time Grubhub customers (limited to one promotional trial per account and household) or existing Grubhub customers who received a direct invite from Grubhub via email or inside the app. Corporate accounts and anyone who previously had a Grubhub+ membership terminated are not eligible.

Grubhub+ is an auto-renewing subscription. Once your free 12-month trial wraps up, your plan will automatically convert to a paid membership at the then-current rate — currently $9.99 per month if you choose monthly billing at sign-up, or $90 per year if you pick annual billing, plus tax.

Even with $0 delivery fees, additional charges such as reduced service fees, driver benefits fees, small order fees, or distance and weather fees may still apply depending on the order.

If you are new to Grubhub — or spotted an invite sitting in your inbox — signing up before Dec. 7 is an easy way to dodge delivery fees all year long. Just remember to cancel before month 13 hits.

Cyber Monday takes place on the Monday following Thanksgiving. This year, the shopping event takes place on Monday, Nov. 30. While Cyber Monday originally began as an online counterpart to in-person shopping on Black Friday, the two events have merged into an extended online shopping bonanza.

Amazon: Amazon recently announced that its Black Friday sale will begin on Nov. 19, with new deals dropping through Cyber Monday, on Nov. 30.

Walmart: Walmart has three major sale events throughout November: the early Black Friday sale from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15, the Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26), and the online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

#415. Bartesian Discount Codes: 35% Off

Bartesian is the Keurig of cocktails. After trying several automatic cocktail makers on the market, it was the only cocktail maker I could see fitting into my normal routine. It works like any capsule-style device, but with booze. You fill the Bartesian’s glass bottles with your liquor of choice, make sure there’s water in the reservoir, plop in a cocktail capsule (these typically cost $2-3), choose your drink strength, press “mix,” and then a drink comes out. (If you’ve got kids, the Bartesian Professional version comes with a lock that will stymie curious fingers.)

Do you need a Bartesian to make cocktails? Of course you don’t. You can dump tequila into sour mix anytime and call it a margarita. But perhaps you’d like to make an espresso martini, a blackberry margarita, and also a Long Island Iced Tea? The Bartesian is a sort of shortcut to a home bar, without having to store all the mixers—and a bit of a novelty. It will be fun, and silly, and the drinks are kind of fine in a Spring Break way: strong and sweet and with sometimes fun flavors. Don’t expect sophistication. #414. JPMorgan Chase says temporary software bug is affecting consumer banking

JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.

"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC.

"This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today."

CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved.

Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET.

A representative for U.S. Bank said that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays."

Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan.

The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

— CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

#410. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

#406. Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs."

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy."

"They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth."

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

"The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded."

The company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said.

Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits."

The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5."

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

The company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

"Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses."

Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

"There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he said. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that plans and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World."

The entertainment company has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously announced a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

#403. Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations

Home Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.

Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.

Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.

"I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan."

McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.

"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.

He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.

Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.

Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.

The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.

#399. Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years

Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth."

Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve."

"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said.

He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also said Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.

Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the company sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.

He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.

"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he said.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

#396. Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions."

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

#395. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 24, 2026

The Full Moon is here, and this one's a Supermoon. That means the Moon is closer to Earth than usual, making it appear slightly bigger and brighter in the night sky.

As of Tuesday, Nov. 24, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Full Moon phase, with 100% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Crisium, as well as the Copernicus Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Archimedes Crater, the Endymion Crater, and the Alphonsus Crater. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 15 landing spot, the Schiller Crater, and the Rima Hyginus.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

It takes around 29.5 days for the Moon to move through all its phases, according to NASA. Throughout this period, the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun determines how much of its illuminated surface we can see. Starting with a New Moon, the visible portion gradually increases until it reaches a Full Moon, before shrinking again as the cycle comes back around.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.
